notes.meaning: Solomon decides to test whether pure pleasure and good times can bring true happiness. He talks directly to his own heart, setting up a deliberate experiment with luxury and fun. In the end, he discovers that chasing pleasure is completely empty, like trying to grab the wind.

Loud parties and constant joking are examined next and judged to be pointless madness. Shallow laughter might briefly distract a person, but it cannot heal a hurting heart or solve life's deep problems. When the noise dies down, nothing of lasting value has been gained.

The king tries cheering his body with fine wine while keeping his mind alert and thoughtful. He does not become a reckless drunkard; instead, he uses wisdom to steer his experiment and observe what actually brings satisfaction. He wants to know what ordinary people should spend their short earthly lives doing.

Solomon turns to grand creative projects, building royal palaces and planting lush vineyards. He designs magnificent parks filled with all kinds of fruit trees, along with huge stone pools to water them. These vast works brought real artistic satisfaction, yet they were built mainly to see if human achievement could satisfy the soul.

The king surrounds himself with immense wealth, thousands of servants, and royal singers for entertainment. He gathers tribute and treasures from other kings and provinces across his empire, exceeding everyone before him in Jerusalem. He even gathers many concubines to satisfy every romantic and sensual desire.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that the rare Hebrew words at the end of the verse are difficult to translate; while many ancient versions suggested musical instruments or cup-bearers, the context of royal luxury strongly supports concubines or ladies of the harem.

notes.meaning: Solomon grows greater in fame, wealth, and power than anyone who had ever ruled in Jerusalem before him. Through it all, his sharp mind and God-given wisdom stay with him, allowing him to examine his experiences clearly. He never loses his ability to step back and weigh the true worth of everything he possesses.

Whatever caught Solomon's eye or stirred his interest, he gave to himself without holding back. He enjoyed the excitement of hard work and tasted the immediate rewards of all his big projects. That temporary thrill of accomplishment was real, but it was the only earthly reward his labor could give.

When Solomon steps back to look at everything his hands had built and all the energy he had spent, the excitement fades away. Viewed on its own terms without an eternal purpose, the whole enterprise feels empty and like chasing the wind. None of his massive achievements provided lasting peace or permanent gain under the sun.

Solomon pauses to compare wisdom, reckless living, and simple foolishness side by side. He knows that no future king will ever have more wealth, power, or opportunity to test these things than he already had. If the greatest king on earth could not find ultimate meaning in them, no one who comes after him will either.

The Teacher sees that wisdom is clearly better than foolishness, shining like bright daylight compared to pitch-black darkness. A wise person uses good judgment and sees where they are walking, while a fool stumbles along blindly into trouble. Yet despite this real advantage, one unavoidable event—physical death—catches up to both of them in the end.

Solomon realizes that the very same death awaiting the foolish will overtake him, the wisest of men. This thought leads him to question the earthly value of his great learning and careful living. If wisdom cannot rescue a person from the grave, then earthly wisdom by itself cannot be life's ultimate answer.

Time eventually erases the memory of both the wise thinker and the reckless fool. Future generations will move on, and almost all earthly accomplishments will be forgotten. It grieves Solomon deeply that the wise man must die just like the fool, with neither able to escape being swallowed up by time.

Faced with this harsh reality, Solomon feels a heavy disgust toward earthly life. All human striving under the sun feels like a painful burden because death cancels it all out. Looking at the world purely through an earthly lens leaves the heart feeling empty and discouraged.

The king begins to hate all the great wealth and property he worked so hard to build, because he must leave everything behind when he dies. Worse still, he has no way of knowing whether his heir will manage it wisely or squander it like a fool. Yet that successor will control every single thing Solomon skillfully accomplished.

Solomon lets his heart sink into deep sorrow over all his exhausting labor. He stops hoping that his earthly work can give him lasting satisfaction or secure his future. Letting go of false hopes in worldly success is painful, but it clears the way to look beyond earthly things.

A person can work all his days with skill, wisdom, and honesty, only to leave his hard-earned life's work to someone who never lifted a finger for it. The heir receives the reward without any of the sweat or discipline. Solomon calls this unfair reality a heavy evil and a deeply frustrating part of life.

Solomon asks what a worker truly gains after pouring a lifetime of anxious effort into his work. Day after day brings grief and heavy burdens, and even late at night his mind cannot rest from worrying about his responsibilities. Without God at the center, endless striving for success only produces stress and sleepless nights.

The Teacher now turns toward hope by pointing out that eating, drinking, and enjoying one's daily work are good things. These simple everyday blessings do not happen by accident; they are gracious gifts given straight from the hand of God. When received with a thankful heart, ordinary labor and meals bring real joy.

differ.view: Work and enjoying its fruit are creational gifts from God given before the Fall, meant to be embraced gladly as service to the Lord rather than treated as mere drudgery.
This counsel is primarily advice on making the best of a difficult, fallen world under the sun, showing that simple pleasures are gifts of God even though they do not give ultimate eternal meaning.

notes.meaning: No one can truly taste food or experience deep satisfaction in life apart from God's personal blessing. Solomon had every luxury available to him, yet he learned that earthly things cannot satisfy by themselves. Genuine contentment is not something we can force; it is an ability God must give.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Greek and Syriac manuscripts read 'apart from Him' rather than 'more than I', highlighting that true enjoyment is impossible without God's enabling grace.

notes.meaning: God gives wisdom, knowledge, and genuine joy to the person who walks in a way that pleases Him. Meanwhile, the ungodly person is left with the exhausting chore of piling up wealth, only to have God hand it over to someone who honors Him. Yet when viewed strictly from an earthly standpoint, hoarding possessions without God remains an empty chase after the wind.
